newsitem.title: INDIA: India shares seen cautious on political woes.
newsitem.headline: India shares seen cautious on political woes.

text.p: Indian stocks are seen opening cautiously on Friday as investors focus on politics, analysts said.
The benchmark 30-share Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) index finished down 24.56 points, or 0.58 percent, at 4,226.57 after staying in positive territory for most of the day.
"I see the market opening cautiously, maybe a little weaker," said Antony Sequeira, managing director of Arcadia Share and Stock Brokers Ltd.
Traders said the markets would closely watch political developments arising from the possible arrest of a key political leader in eastern Bihar state.

An Indian court on Thursday denied a request by Laloo Prasad Yadav, the state's chief minister, for legal protection against arrest in a $280-million corruption scandal case that has caused rifts in the ruling centre-left coalition.
"Nervousness? Definitely," said Chandresh Kampani, a partner in brokerage Jamnadas Morarjee & Company. "Political uncertainty is worrying, but I don't think this will cause much damage."
Yadav, until recently the president of Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's Janata Dal party, broke away to form a regional group but at least three of his supporters remain in the Indian cabinet.
The court order came minutes before parliament began a scheduled discussion on the scandal, over which both the houses witnessed uproarious scenes on Wednesday and Thursday.
Yadav says he is innocent and will not resign from his post. His stand has provoked a major national debate on corruption and posed a political challenge to Gujral's United Front coalition.
Kampani said the 15-party coalition government's future depended on how long it enjoyed the support of the Congress Party, which has the second largest number of seats in parliament.
Analysts said the political problems have resulted in a slowdown in foreign portfolio inflows, but they do not see a sell-off.
But some analysts said the market was over-reacting to Yadav's possible arrest.
"I don't see it'll strike at the core of political stability," said Maulik Sharedalal, a member-broker at the BSE. "He might be isolated. It might put to rest uncertainty fears."
